strengths: Original and potentially useful idea: MAPR creates verifiable auxiliary targets from solution-rollout statistics—difficulty, correct-solution length, and notions—and reuses these predictions for gating and early stopping.
The empirical scope is substantial: experiments cover Qwen3 at three scales, two additional model families, both GRPO and DAPO, six mathematical benchmarks, and several out-of-domain evaluations.
The main mathematical results are broadly consistent. MAPR improves average Pass@1 across all three Qwen3 scales, with especially notable absolute gains on AIME and OlympiadBench for the 4B model.
The paper evaluates practical training efficiency using wall-clock time rather than token counts alone. Figure 4 suggests that MAPR-efficient reaches the GRPO endpoint accuracy appreciably earlier.
Several relevant ablations are included, covering reward components, meta-rollout count, difficulty-reward scaling, gating threshold, cutoff margin, transition step, and notion feed-in.

The method and meta-prediction prompt are explained clearly, and the appendix provides the reward-scoring code. The manuscript is generally readable and visually organized. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/a1eeb5d7449243fc829aff687664db9b/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central causal claim that meta-awareness "directly enhances" reasoning is not established. The analysis in Figure 3 compares two endogenous quantities that improve during the same training run; reward calibration, model quality, and training time are all jointly determined. Using absolute reward differences and a linear/Shapley analysis does not remove this confounding. Matched controls such as shuffled prediction targets, an equally costly generic auxiliary task, or freezing/transferring the predictor are needed.

The comparison does not cleanly isolate MAPR from additional supervision and optimization. MAPR adds eight meta-rollouts and associated policy-gradient updates, amounting to 15.5% of reported rollout tokens, but Table 1 compares equal epochs rather than equal compute. Figure 4 partially addresses wall-clock compute, yet the batching, parallelization, hardware, and treatment of gated prompts are not specified well enough to verify the comparison.

Reported uncertainty is over 32 evaluation samples, not independent training runs. No training-seed variance or statistical tests are provided. This is particularly problematic for small benchmarks such as AIME and for the mostly one-point or smaller out-of-domain improvements, which may be sampling noise.

The notion mechanism is insufficiently validated and may explain gains without supporting a meta-awareness interpretation. Its reward merely favors predicted strings occurring more in correct than incorrect rollouts; this can act as semantic auxiliary training or solution-feature distillation. The text claims lemma-based matching, whereas the supplied code uses raw substring matching. There is no systematic audit of extracted notions, reward hacking, list length, or sensitivity to paraphrases.

Important implementation details are missing: how solution and meta losses are combined and weighted, whether gated examples are replaced to preserve batch size and update count, the chosen default values of the gating threshold and cutoff multiplier, hardware and parallelism, training seeds, and precise construction of Pass@8 and its deviations. The abstract's code link is blank, so the stated public implementation is not actually accessible from the submission.

Some evidence is described more strongly than it supports. In Figure 5, correct-rollout standardized errors have a displayed mean of 5.55 rather than being centered near zero as claimed. Predictive-gating labels are themselves finite-rollout estimates of zero variance, and no confidence intervals or downstream error-cost analysis is given.

Static gating permanently excludes prompts judged trivial or impossible even though the policy and its competence change during training. The paper acknowledges this design but does not measure false exclusions over time or whether gating harms learning on initially difficult examples.

The claimed inference-efficiency and environmental benefits are not experimentally demonstrated: the proposed gating and cutoff experiments concern post-training, and no inference latency, token use, energy, or emissions are reported.

There is no substantive limitations section. Risks from benchmark or training-data overlap, dependence on rule-verifiable tasks, noisy self-generated targets, verifier errors, and transfer beyond mathematics are not adequately discussed. Cross-domain notion generality is supported only by a few selected examples, while ethics and dual-use considerations receive only a cursory statement.

strengths: The core idea—training a shared policy to predict rollout difficulty, successful-solution length, and useful notions, then using those predictions for gating and cutoff—is intuitive and potentially useful for reasoning-model post-training.

The empirical scope is broader than a single benchmark: Table 1 covers six mathematics benchmarks and three Qwen3 sizes, while Tables 6–8 include DAPO, Llama/Gemma models, and out-of-domain evaluations. Several gains are substantial, especially for Qwen3-4B on AIME.

The paper reports component, rollout-count, transition-step, and reward-base ablations. It also measures predictive-gating precision/recall and accounts for the additional meta-rollout tokens, which are useful attempts to characterize the method rather than reporting endpoint accuracy alone.

The overall pipeline and reward definitions are mostly understandable, and the appendix supplies the meta-prediction prompt and a reward-code snippet. The work combines self-prediction and compute control in a way that has some originality, even though it is closely related to existing difficulty-aware budgeting and metacognitive-training work.
weaknesses: The central causal claim that meta-awareness “directly enhances” reasoning is not supported. Figure 3 correlates checkpoint-to-checkpoint changes in prediction reward with accuracy while both evolve during training; using |Δr_pred| further discards direction. The Shapley-R² analysis remains correlational. Neither analysis separates genuine metacognition from ordinary auxiliary-task training, extra math-related supervision, or changes in policy state. A matched-compute auxiliary objective, shuffled-target control, or intervention based on held-out calibration would be needed.

The evaluation does not report independent training seeds. The stated standard deviations are over 32 inference samplings from a single trained checkpoint, so they do not quantify RL training instability. This is especially consequential for the smaller improvements on Qwen3-14B, DAPO, Llama, Gemma, and the out-of-domain benchmarks; several alternative-family results are tiny or mixed.

The compute-efficiency evidence is insufficiently specified. The claimed 1.28× speedup relies on a single wall-clock plot without hardware, run-to-run variability, profiling, or a precise derivation. MAPR adds eight meta rollouts per prompt, while MAPR-efficient changes which prompts and trajectories are processed; the manuscript does not fully specify batching/update accounting needed to establish a fair equal-compute comparison.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the main claims. The promised public code link is blank, and the reward snippet is not a complete implementation. Exact selected values and operational details for σ_PG and l_LC, parsing/failure handling, solution prompts, static-gating bookkeeping, hardware, random seeds, and evaluation aggregation are missing or unclear.

There are discrepancies between the specification and supplied code: the paper describes lemma-based notion matching, but the code performs case-sensitive substring matching; the length equation uses inclusive bounds, whereas the code uses strict inequalities. The notion reward is consequently easy to confound with wording and response length and does not robustly establish concept-level awareness.

Some headline reporting is internally inconsistent. For Qwen3-4B, the reported averages increase from 42.49 to 49.48, which is 6.99 percentage points or about 16.45% relative, not the claimed 13.04%. The abstract presents that erroneous number as a principal result. Out-of-domain gains are mostly small and are reported without uncertainty, yet are described as consistent enhanced generalization.

The framing overstates the supervision advantage: MAPR still requires ground-truth answers and a rule-based correctness verifier to construct its meta targets, so it does not eliminate external supervision in the ordinary sense. It only avoids separately annotated meta-awareness labels.

Presentation is readable at a high level, but several figures are too small or underspecified, and terms such as “difficulty,” “meta-awareness,” and “knowledge boundary” are treated as interchangeable without validating the construct. The paper also lacks an honest limitations discussion covering single-run evidence, dependence on verifiable-answer datasets, noisy substring-based notion rewards, static exclusion of prompts, and possible distributional bias from labeling difficult prompts “unsolvable.” The impact statement asserts environmental benefits without an energy analysis and does not discuss reliability or fairness risks from erroneous gating. These evidential and reproducibility problems prevent acceptance despite the promising idea.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/65ffab9db6264608a12b29f149a60348/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} presents a useful and original idea: training a reasoning model to predict statistics of its own solution rollouts—success rate, correct-solution length, and employed notions—and verifying those predictions without separately curated meta-cognition labels.

The empirical results are broad and generally favorable. MAPR improves Pass@1 and Pass@8 across three Qwen3 sizes and six mathematics benchmarks, with especially large gains for Qwen3-4B; it also improves a DAPO baseline and transfers, though less strongly, to Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-9B.

The work connects its auxiliary predictions to practical training controls. Predictive gating and early cutoff are intuitive uses of the learned signals, and the reported 0.9065 F1 for detecting zero-variance prompts plus the wall-clock/accuracy trade-off suggest genuine efficiency potential.

The paper includes useful component studies covering the three reward terms, the number of meta rollouts, reward scaling, gating/cutoff settings, transition time, notion feed-in, model families, and RL algorithms. The supplied prompt and reward-code excerpt further clarify the core implementation.

Presentation is mostly clear and well organized, with readable equations, diagrams, and tables. The environmental motivation and brief dual-use discussion are appropriate; the method raises no obvious unresolved ethical concern beyond the usual risks of improving general-purpose reasoning models.
weaknesses: The claim that meta-awareness “directly” causes the performance gains is not established. Figure 3 compares quantities that co-evolve along the same training trajectory, while the Shapley-R² analysis is an observational linear decomposition of correlated checkpoint features. Better policy states can simultaneously yield higher accuracy and better predictions, so neither analysis separates meta-awareness from training progress or shared model quality. A controlled intervention—such as shuffled or stop-gradient meta-targets, a matched auxiliary-task control, or manipulation of calibration at fixed checkpoints—is needed for the causal wording.

The statistical evidence is weaker than the tables initially suggest. Reported deviations are over 32 inference samples rather than independent training runs, and the paper does not report multiple RL seeds or uncertainty over trained checkpoints. This matters because several gains, especially on alternative model families and out-of-domain tasks, are small and plausibly within run-to-run training variation.

Compute comparisons are insufficiently controlled and documented. MAPR adds eight long meta rollouts per prompt, yet Figure 4 alone does not explain hardware utilization, parallelism, token throughput, or repeated-run variability. Comparisons against simple compute-matched auxiliary prediction, curriculum, historical pass-rate gating, or length heuristics are absent, making it unclear how much benefit is specific to the proposed notion of meta-awareness rather than extra training signal or better sample selection.

Some reward definitions are weak proxies for calibrated self-knowledge. The binary length reward accepts any value inside the observed min–max range, which may be broad and unstable when few rollouts are correct. The notion reward relies on lexical occurrence and can favor generic or easily matched terms; moreover, the prose mentions lemma matching whereas the supplied code performs direct substring matching. These issues leave room for reward gaming and undermine the interpretation of the learned behavior as meta-awareness.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The displayed public-code link is blank, only the reward function is included, and exact default values for key MAPR-efficient settings are not stated unambiguously. Hardware, random seeds, checkpoint-selection rules, full solution/evaluation prompts, gating prevalence, and detailed wall-clock accounting are also missing. Thus reproducing the headline speedup and distinguishing implementation effects would be difficult.

Several conclusions are overstated. The framework still relies on answer ground truth and rule-based verification for solution rollouts, so claims of eliminating external supervision require qualification. Likewise, the out-of-domain improvements are mostly small and lack uncertainty, and no contamination analysis is provided for widely used benchmarks. The paper would benefit from an explicit limitations section acknowledging proxy validity, static gating potentially discarding tasks that become learnable later, benchmark scope, and training-run variance.
